title: THE MESSIAH ENTERED A FAMILY HISTORY CONTAINING ADULTERY, PROSTITUTION, BETRAYAL, AND MURDER
paragraphs: THE MESSIAH ENTERED A FAMILY HISTORY CONTAINING ADULTERY, PROSTITUTION, BETRAYAL, AND MURDER
Before Jesus ever carried a cross, His genealogy carried names most families would have tried to hide—and Matthew refused to erase a single scar.
There are things families do not put in the Christmas letter.
Names that become whispers.
Stories that suddenly go quiet when the children enter the room.
The uncle nobody mentions.
The marriage that collapsed.
The betrayal everyone remembers but nobody discusses.
The addiction.
The affair.
The prison sentence.
The pregnancy.
The abandonment.
The night somebody made a decision that changed an entire family.
Maybe your family has one of those stories.
Maybe you are one of those stories.
And perhaps that is why the opening chapter of the New Testament is far more breathtaking than most people realize.
We often rush through Matthew 1 because it looks like a list.
Abraham fathered Isaac.
Isaac fathered Jacob.
Jacob fathered Judah.
Name after name.
Generation after generation.
But Matthew is not merely recording ancestry.
He is opening a graveyard of family memories and announcing that the Messiah walked straight into it.
The Greek words opening the Gospel are striking:
“Βίβλος γενέσεως Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ…”
Biblos geneseōs Iēsou Christou…
“The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ…”
Matthew 1:1.
And then Matthew begins naming people.
Real people.
Not polished religious characters invented to make Jesus appear respectable.
People whose stories include faith and failure, courage and cowardice, righteousness and devastating sin.

Matthew identifies Jesus as the Son of David and the Son of Abraham, placing Him squarely within Israel’s covenant history. Then, unusually for an ancient genealogy of this kind, Matthew draws attention to several women: Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, “the wife of Uriah,” and finally Mary.
And suddenly the genealogy begins to bleed.
“Tamar.”
If you know Genesis 38, you know that this name carries an uncomfortable story.

Judah had failed in his responsibility toward Tamar. After the deaths of her husbands Er and Onan, Judah promised his son Shelah to her but did not fulfill what he had promised. Tamar eventually disguised herself, Judah unknowingly slept with her, and she became pregnant by him.
When Judah later learned that Tamar was pregnant, his first response was horrifyingly hypocritical: judgment.
Then Tamar produced the identifying items Judah himself had given her.
And Judah was forced to confront himself.
His confession in Hebrew contains words that should haunt every self-righteous heart:
“צָדְקָה מִמֶּנִּי”
Tsadqah mimmenni.
“She is more righteous than I.”
Genesis 38:26.
Judah had been prepared to condemn publicly what he had participated in privately.
Sound familiar?
Human beings have not changed very much.
We are remarkably skilled at becoming furious over another person's visible failure while protecting our own hidden compromises.
We compare sins.
Categorize sinners.
Manage reputations.
And sometimes the thing we hate most in another person is frighteningly close to something we refuse to confront in ourselves.
But Tamar's story does not disappear.
Matthew writes her name.
“Judah fathered Perez and Zerah by Tamar.”
There she is.
Inside the genealogy of Jesus Christ.
Then another name appears.
Rahab.
This time Scripture is unmistakably explicit about her former occupation.
Joshua 2:1 describes Rahab with the Hebrew expression:
“אִשָּׁה זוֹנָה”
ishah zonah.
A woman who was a prostitute.
The New Testament does not sanitize that history either. Hebrews 11:31 remembers Rahab while also celebrating the faith that caused her to receive the Israelite spies in peace.
Think about that.
God did not need Matthew to rewrite Rahab's résumé before putting her name into the genealogy.
Grace did something infinitely greater.
God rewrote her future.
Rahab lived in Jericho, a city marked for judgment. Yet she had heard what the God of Israel had done, and she confessed something astonishing:
“The LORD your God, he is God in heaven above, and in earth beneath.”
Joshua 2:11.
She believed.
She acted upon that belief.
The scarlet cord appeared in the window.
Judgment came.
Jericho fell.
And Rahab lived.
But her story did not merely end with survival.
Matthew tells us:
“Salmon fathered Boaz by Rahab.”
Rahab entered Israel's story.
Then Boaz fathered Obed.
Obed fathered Jesse.
Jesse fathered David.
And generations later…
Jesus.
The woman once known by her prostitution became an ancestor named in the genealogy of the Messiah.
That does not mean prostitution was good.
It means grace is greater.
That distinction matters.
The Gospel never requires us to rename darkness as light.
Jesus does something better.
He saves sinners from darkness.
Grace does not say sin does not matter.
The cross proves precisely how much sin matters.
Grace says sin does not get the final word over the person who comes to God in faith.
Keep reading Matthew.
Eventually you reach the king everyone recognizes.
David.
The shepherd.
The psalmist.
The giant killer.
The man after God's own heart.
The king.
Surely Matthew will allow David's glorious reputation to carry the story forward.
But Matthew does something startling.
He writes:
He could simply have written “Bathsheba.”
Instead, the Greek preserves the uncomfortable reminder:
“ἐκ τῆς τοῦ Οὐρίου”
ek tēs tou Ouriou.
Literally, “by/from the [woman] of Uriah.”
Uriah.
The dead man still has a name.
Matthew will not let David's crown bury Uriah's blood.
Because behind Solomon's birth stands one of the darkest episodes in David's reign.
Second Samuel 11 records David seeing Bathsheba, taking her, and sleeping with her while her husband Uriah was away fighting in David's army.
Bathsheba became pregnant.
David tried to conceal what had happened.
When Uriah's integrity frustrated David's attempt at concealment, David escalated.
He sent instructions to Joab that Uriah should be placed where the fighting was fiercest and then abandoned so that he would be struck down.
And David sent those instructions through Uriah himself.
Imagine that.
Uriah carried the letter arranging his own death.
The faithful soldier carried his death warrant back to the battlefield, written by the king he served.
Uriah died.
David took Bathsheba as his wife.
From a human perspective, perhaps the scandal could now be contained.
But Scripture delivers one devastating sentence:
“The thing that David had done displeased the LORD.”
2 Samuel 11:27.
Kings can manipulate narratives.
God cannot be manipulated.
David could move soldiers.
He could command generals.
He could hide an affair from a kingdom.
He could not hide from God.
Then Nathan walked into the throne room.
“You are the man.”
And David finally stopped running.
Psalm 51 gives us the sound of a shattered king:
“Have mercy upon me, O God…”
Not, “Protect my reputation.”
Not, “Explain my circumstances.”
Not, “Compare me with somebody worse.”
Mercy.
David finally understood what every sinner must eventually understand.
When you stand guilty before a holy God, your greatest need is not better public relations.
Your greatest need is mercy.
And this is where Matthew's genealogy becomes intensely personal.
Because perhaps you have spent years thinking Christianity belongs to people with cleaner histories than yours.
People who did not do what you did.
People who were not touched by what happened to you.
People whose families do not have those stories.
People who do not wake up at 2:00 in the morning remembering that night.
People who do not carry shame into church.
People who do not delete browser histories.
People who do not hide messages.
People who do not secretly wonder whether God would still want them if everybody knew the truth.
Read Matthew 1 again.
Slowly.
Tamar.
Rahab.
David.
The wife of Uriah.
Matthew does not airbrush the family tree before introducing Jesus.
He places Jesus at the end of a genealogy containing human sin, suffering, outsiders, failures, kings, ordinary people, exile, brokenness, and astonishing providence.
Then comes the name toward which the entire genealogy has been moving.
Jesus.
“Ἰησοῦς.”
Iēsous.
The Greek form corresponding to the Hebrew/Aramaic name Yeshua.
And Matthew immediately explains the theological significance of His name:
“You shall call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins.”
Matthew 1:21.
There it is.
Not save His people because they never sinned.
Save His people from their sins.
That is why the genealogy matters.
The Savior entered a world that desperately needed saving.

Jesus did not become morally contaminated by the sins committed by people in His human ancestry. Scripture presents Him as the sinless Son of God. He did not inherit their guilt or participate in their rebellion.
He entered their history.
That difference is everything.
The Holy One stepped into the story of sinners without becoming sinful Himself.
And eventually He walked toward another piece of wood.
Not Rahab's window.
Not David's throne.
A cross.
There the scandal becomes almost unbearable.
The One without sin stands where sinners belong.
The innocent One is condemned.
The righteous One is mocked.
The Creator is pierced by His creatures.
The Son of God carries judgment.
And the blood that falls from Calvary does what no family secret, religious performance, self-improvement plan, motivational speech, or carefully manufactured reputation could ever accomplish.
It cleanses sinners.
This is the Gospel.
Not that your past never happened.
Not that your sin was insignificant.
Not that your wounds were imaginary.
Not that evil should be excused.
The Gospel is that Jesus Christ entered human history, lived without sin, died for sinners, and rose again—and everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith finds forgiveness and new life in Him.
Your sin may explain part of your history.
It does not have to own your eternity.
Your family may have handed you wounds.
Those wounds do not have authority to become your identity.
Maybe your father failed you.
Maybe your mother disappeared emotionally.
Maybe somebody betrayed you.
Maybe you betrayed somebody.
Maybe you crossed a line you swore you would never cross.
Maybe everyone thinks you are strong because you have become extraordinarily skilled at bleeding silently.
Maybe your greatest fear is not that people hate you.
It is that they would hate you if they actually knew you.
Jesus already knows.
That should terrify us if we intend to cling to our sin.
But for the repentant sinner, it becomes breathtakingly beautiful.
Because the One who knows the whole truth is the very One calling sinners to Himself.
You do not have to clean the genealogy before coming to Christ.
You come to Christ because you cannot clean yourself.
Repentance is not pretending the past did not happen.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Savior.
Grace is not God's permission to remain chained.
Grace breaks chains.
Forgiveness is not Jesus telling you that your sin was harmless.
Forgiveness cost Him blood.
And transformation is not learning to hide more successfully.
It is learning to walk in the light.
Maybe that is why this genealogy feels so different once you actually see it.
It is no longer a boring list of names.
It becomes evidence.
Evidence that God works through catastrophically imperfect human history without ever becoming the author or approver of human evil.
Evidence that shame cannot outmaneuver providence.
Evidence that outsiders can be brought near.
Evidence that repentance is possible.
Evidence that failure does not make redemption impossible.
Evidence that the Savior did not wait for humanity to become respectable before entering our story.
He came because we weren't.
And maybe right now there is one name you keep thinking about.
Yours.
You can understand grace for Rahab.
Grace for David.
Grace for Peter.
Grace for the thief dying beside Jesus.
Grace for everybody except yourself.
But the Gospel will not allow you to make your sin more powerful than Christ's ability to save.
Do not misunderstand that sentence.
There is no salvation in merely feeling emotional about Jesus.
There is no salvation in admiring redemption while refusing repentance.
Christ calls us to Himself.
Come out of hiding.
Confess.
Turn.
Believe.
Follow Him.
Maybe your prayer has become complicated because you think you need beautiful religious words.
You don't.
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
“Jesus, forgive me.”
“Jesus, I have been hiding.”
“Jesus, I need You.”
A broken sinner calling upon a merciful Savior does not need impressive vocabulary.
You need Christ.
And if something inside you has been exposed while reading this, do not rush past it.
Be honest.
Not because typing words underneath an article saves anyone.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes confession begins when somebody finally stops pretending.
And somebody else reading your comment may realize they are not the only person fighting to come back into the light.
If you know someone who believes their past has disqualified them from the love of God, send this to them.
Not as content.
As a lifeline.
Christ alone saves.
Giving and supporting Christian ministry should come freely from gratitude and conviction, never manipulation or fear.
The Gospel is bigger than our platform.
Invite your family.
Invite the believer who has grown cold.
Invite the exhausted Christian.
Invite the seeker.
Invite the person who does not believe yet.
Invite the person convinced church is filled only with people pretending to have perfect histories.
Let them meet Tamar.
Let them meet Rahab.
Let them hear Uriah's name.
Let them watch David collapse under conviction.
And then…
let them meet Jesus.
Because that is where Matthew was taking us all along.
Not ultimately to Tamar.
Not to Rahab.
Not to David.
Not even to the scandal.
To Christ.
Maybe your history contains things you wish you could erase.
Maybe there are chapters you would burn if life were a book.
But the astonishing announcement of Christianity is not that Jesus gives you permission to pretend those pages never existed.
He offers something far more powerful.
Redemption.
The Bible does not hide the scandal.
It reveals the Savior.
The Bible does not pretend sinners are innocent.
It announces that the guilty can be justified through Christ.
The Bible does not teach that broken people can repair themselves if they simply become inspirational enough.
It tells broken people to come to Jesus.
So come.
With the history.
With the regret.
With the secret.
With the consequences.
With the wounds somebody else gave you.
With the sins you chose yourself.
Come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come believing that the blood of Jesus is stronger than the stain you thought would define you forever.
Because Matthew's genealogy whispers something before Jesus ever preaches His first sermon:
God is not intimidated by ruined histories.
He knows how to bring redemption into places human beings thought were beyond recovery.
And then the cross shouts what the genealogy whispered.
Grace has a name.
His name is Jesus.
Share that name.
Speak that name.
Build your life around that name.
And when shame tries to introduce you by your worst chapter, remember the genealogy that introduced the Savior.
Your darkest chapter may be part of your history—but when Jesus becomes Lord of your life, your darkest chapter does not get to write the ending.
